 Davis Cup Final 8 2026: the complete guide to the eight teams heading to Bologna
 Originally posted on
 TennisUpToDate.com 
 By Cristhián Avila
  | 
 Last updated Oct 26, 2026 10:03 PM ET
 Add us as a preferred source on Google
  The Davis Cup Final 8 returns to the SuperTennis Arena in Bologna from November 24 to 29, with a very different outlook from the one that has seen Italy dominate the competition over the past three years. The host nation is the defending champion and will be chasing a fourth consecutive title.  
 Italy's 2-0 victory over Spain in the 2025 final made it the first country to win three straight Davis Cup titles since the United States in 1972. However, Jannik Sinner, who has been central to that success, is sidelined with a right knee problem, leaving Flavio Cobolli to lead the Italian challenge.
 His absence opens the door for the other contenders. Carlos Alcaraz leads Spain's squad and will team up with the highly promising Rafael Jódar, with the pair set to make their first appearance together. Alexander Zverev spearheads Germany's challenge and is set to take over the world No. 1 ranking before the tournament begins. Italy, meanwhile, will also be without Matteo Berrettini , although its squad still boasts several high-profile names.
 The result is an unusually open field, with no outright favourite and several nations capable of lifting the trophy.
 View this post on Instagram 
 A post shared by Davis Cup (@daviscup) 
 Czechia, led by Jakub Mensik ; Canada, featuring Félix Auger-Aliassime; and Great Britain, spearheaded by Arthur Fery, may face a tougher path to the title, but all three have the potential to make a run.
 South Korea and Austria, meanwhile, stand out as potential surprise packages. Neither boasts a squad packed with major stars, but both have demonstrated the strength of their collective effort by reaching the Final 8 and exceeding expectations heading into the end of the season.
 This guide breaks down all eight teams, quarterfinal by quarterfinal, examining their player rankings and assessing each matchup.
 How the Final 8 works
 The event is played entirely indoors on hard courts. Each tie takes place over a single day and consists of two singles matches, followed by a doubles match if the teams are level at 1-1. The singles begin with each nation's No. 2 player before the top-ranked players face off in the second match.
 This format makes the depth of each squad crucial: the second singles player and the doubles pairing can be just as decisive as the headline name, allowing a team with two strong singles options and a reliable doubles combination to overcome a side built around a single star.
 The four seeds, as determined following the draw, are Italy (1), Spain (2), Germany (3) and Czechia (4).
 However, captains retain considerable flexibility when selecting their lineups, allowing them to account for current form, matchups and tactical considerations. Spain captain David Ferrer faces an intriguing selection dilemma over who should open the singles campaign against Italy: Rafael Jódar or Alejandro Davidovich Fokina. Both recently reached the Shanghai Masters final, although Jódar holds the higher ranking. Davidovich Fokina's greater experience at the highest level, combined with his recent Masters 1000 title, could nevertheless give him the edge.
 Other teams appear to have clearer plans. Canada's singles order, for example, seems more straightforward, with Denis Shapovalov expected to play first before Félix Auger-Aliassime takes the court in the second singles match. That arrangement would give Canada a strong option in both positions, while preserving the possibility of relying on its doubles pairing if the tie goes down to a decider.

 The favorites: who looks strongest on paper
 Spain is the most complete team on paper. It boasts world No. 3 Carlos Alcaraz and two other top-15 players in Rafael Jódar (No. 11) and Alejandro Davidovich Fokina (No. 15), giving it a level of depth unmatched by any other team in the field. If having a seven-time major champion were not enough to intimidate the opposition, the presence of both recent Shanghai Masters finalists further strengthens Spain's chances under captain David Ferrer. Spain has three top-15 players in its squad, while some of the other nations in the Final 8 do not have a single player ranked that highly.
 Italy presents a more complicated case. The defending champions have the experience of three consecutive titles and the advantage of playing at home, but without Jannik Sinner, their hopes will rest on Flavio Cobolli (No. 6), Luciano Darderi (No. 23) and Lorenzo Musetti (No. 26). They also have an especially strong doubles pairing in Andrea Vavassori and Simone Bolelli, who have extensive experience playing together and winning major titles.
 Italy's draw offers a relatively favourable opening tie, but the path to the title is likely to become much tougher from there. Matteo Berrettini, ranked No. 48, was left out of the squad, with captain Filippo Volandri explaining that the selection was based largely on current rankings.
 Behind Spain and Italy, Czechia and Germany are the two teams best placed to challenge the favourites. The table below compares the top two singles players from each nation.

 Quarterfinal 1: Czechia v Canada, a tie that is closer than it looks
 Czechia, the No. 4 seed coached by Tomas Berdych, qualified by beating the United States 3-2 in Prague. Jiri Lehecka defeated Ben Shelton 6-4, 6-4 in that tie, just five days after Shelton lost the US Open final. The Czechs also have Jakub Mensik, now ranked No. 16, giving them a strong singles pairing. They look more dangerous than their seeding suggests, having already eliminated one of the favourites during the Qualifiers.
 Doubles, however, could be their weakest link. While they have an experienced pairing available for a potential deciding match, it has yet to deliver major results at Grand Slam or Masters 1000 level.
 Canada beat France 3-1 in Quebec City and arrives with Félix Auger-Aliassime, the world No. 7 and the highest-ranked player in this quarterfinal. Denis Shapovalov, currently No. 52, provides a second singles option, with Gabriel Diallo and Liam Draxl also in the squad. If rankings alone determined the outcome, Lehecka could be expected to give Czechia the opening point before Auger-Aliassime levelled the tie, potentially sending the contest to a deciding doubles match. 
 The matchup is not quite that straightforward, however. Lehecka should be favoured against Shapovalov, who has struggled to recapture his best form in recent years. Yet the Canadian's former top-10 status is a reminder of his ability to raise his level on the biggest occasions, even if only for a day. If Shapovalov finds his confidence, he could spring a surprise.
 The second singles match between Mensik and Auger-Aliassime looks even more evenly balanced. Mensik has already shown that he can beat the Tour's biggest names, including Novak Djokovic in the Miami Open final, and was one of only three players to defeat Jannik Sinner in 2026. Indoor hard courts, however, should suit Auger-Aliassime particularly well, making this a difficult matchup to call.
 This could be the closest quarterfinal of the round, with neither team likely to be intimidated by the occasion. Whoever advances would still face a formidable challenge against Italy in the semifinals.

 Quarterfinal 2: Italy v South Korea, the defending champion's soft start
 Italy opens its campaign on Wednesday against South Korea, the surprise qualifier that beat India 3-1 in Seoul. South Korea is the first Asian nation to reach the Final 8 since 2021. Its leading singles player, Kwon Soonwoo, is ranked around No. 157, while Chung Hyeon, a former world No. 19 and 2018 Australian Open semifinalist, has helped the team reach this stage, including by winning a deciding rubber in the Qualifiers against India.
 For Italy, the main storyline is not the opposition but the absence of Jannik Sinner. Flavio Cobolli, the French Open runner-up this season and now the world No. 6, leads the squad, with Luciano Darderi and Lorenzo Musetti providing further singles options. The ranking gap between the two teams is enormous, making this the most lopsided tie on paper. The real test will come in the semifinal against either Czechia or Canada. A convincing opening win would give Italy valuable momentum and send a message to the rest of the field that the absence of Sinner and Matteo Berrettini does not necessarily have to derail its title defence.
 Cobolli showed in 2025 that he could take on a leading role for Italy, and his outstanding 2026 season has raised expectations that he can once again help fill the void left by Sinner. The main selection question concerns the second singles spot: will captain Filippo Volandri turn to Darderi or Musetti? Despite Musetti's slightly lower ranking, his pedigree as a former top-five player and his suitability to indoor hard courts could give him the edge over Darderi, whose game is particularly well suited to clay.
 Whatever the singles lineup, Italy can rely on one of the most established doubles pairings in the competition. Andrea Vavassori and Simone Bolelli have proved their quality repeatedly, offering a reliable option if the tie reaches a deciding rubber. That advantage could prove less significant against teams such as Germany or Great Britain, which also possess strong doubles combinations. Italy should have little trouble overcoming South Korea, but the tie will offer an early indication of how well the defending champions can cope without their biggest star.

 Quarterfinal 3: Great Britain v Germany, the No. 1 in waiting
 Thursday morning's tie pits Germany against Great Britain, with Alexander Zverev set to become world No. 1 by the time the event begins, according to the Associated Press. Great Britain will be led by Arthur Fery (No. 35), a Wimbledon semifinalist this year, and Cameron Norrie (No. 41). The British team qualified by beating Ecuador 4-0 in London, while Germany, the No. 3 seed, secured its place with a 3-1 victory over Croatia in Halle, where Zverev won his singles rubber.
 Germany's squad is built around Zverev and Jan-Lennard Struff (No. 47), with Kevin Krawietz and Tim Pütz forming its doubles pairing. Great Britain's clearest route to an upset is to win the second singles match and take the tie into doubles, where Neal Skupski and Henry Patten could give the team a realistic chance. Germany has a significant advantage in the top singles matchup, but the strength of the British doubles specialists makes a three-rubber contest a plausible scenario.
 Much of the pressure in the opening singles match will fall on Norrie. He faces a more evenly matched contest against Struff, and Britain likely needs that point to keep its hopes alive, given the apparent gap between Fery and Zverev. The conditions could make the top singles matchup even more challenging for the Briton: Zverev will arrive in Bologna just days after competing at the ATP Finals in Turin, meaning he should be among the players best prepared for the indoor courts and conditions in Italy.
 If the tie reaches doubles, the outcome becomes far less predictable. Both nations have specialist pairings, but Skupski and Patten have enjoyed an outstanding season. The question is whether they can carry that form into the Davis Cup while adapting to playing together, a challenge that also faces Krawietz and Pütz. It could be one of the most compelling doubles matchups of the quarterfinals, with Great Britain perhaps holding a slight edge if the tie goes to a decider.
 For Britain, that may be its clearest path to the semifinals against a German team led by the player expected to take over the world No. 1 ranking. Germany remains the favourite, but if Norrie can deliver in the opening singles and the British doubles team maintains its form, an upset is far from impossible.

 Quarterfinal 4: Austria v Spain, Alcaraz's return
 Spain, the 2025 runner-up and the favourite on paper, closes the quarterfinals against Austria, which qualified by beating Belgium 3-1 on indoor clay in Vienna. Jurij Rodionov was the hero of that tie, defeating Gauthier Onclin before overcoming Zizou Bergs, currently ranked No. 39. He leads an Austrian squad that also includes Lukas Neumayer, Joel Schwärzler, Neil Oberleitner and Lucas Miedler, with Jürgen Melzer serving as captain.
 Spain arrives with Carlos Alcaraz, who recently completed the career Grand Slam by winning the Australian Open. The Davis Cup remains one of the few major titles missing from his collection, giving him an additional incentive to lead Spain to the trophy.
 Alcaraz has further motivation to succeed, and Spain looks particularly formidable this year following the emergence of Rafael Jódar and the return of Alejandro Davidovich Fokina, who had been left out of the squad in recent seasons despite spending several years as Spain's No. 2 player. With Jannik Sinner absent from Italy's lineup and other major contenders such as the United States, led by Ben Shelton, and Serbia, featuring Novak Djokovic, also missing, the conditions appear ideal for Alcaraz to capture the title that has eluded him.
 Opening the tie against Austria should not pose a major problem for the Spaniards, who will look to settle the contest in singles. Alcaraz is the clear favourite in his matchup, while Spain should also have the advantage in the second singles, whether captain David Ferrer opts for Jódar or Davidovich Fokina. In doubles, world No. 6 Marcel Granollers provides a reliable option, with Pedro Martínez having proved a capable partner in the past despite not being a specialist in the discipline.
 Austria's task is made even harder by the absence of its top-ranked player, Sebastian Ofner, who is sidelined through injury. If Spain advances, however, the challenge could become considerably tougher in the semifinals, where a potential meeting with Zverev's Germany awaits. Even so, few teams in the draw look capable of taking a singles point from Spain, making the 2025 runners-up strong contenders to reach the final once again.
